cards.explanation: The practical sequence includes extraction, amplification, checking products and sequencing.
cards.text: Molecular genetic testing connects a patient sample to a clinically interpreted {{c1::result}}.

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 6
slides.text:
1. SAMPLE COLLECTION
Obtaining DNA
Samples for DNA extraction are acquired from the patient using one of several methods

The method depends on various factors, especially the age of the patient

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 7
slides.text:
2. DNA EXTRACTION
Breaking and entering
DNA is safely stored behind two membranes, the cellular and the nuclear

The cell houses many other components as well, including organelles, RNA, proteins etc.

How do we gain access to the DNA while getting rid of all the other cellular components?

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 8
slides.text:
2. DNA EXTRACTION
Time for cleaning
In a chemical approach to DNA extraction, we use a detergent to rupture the cell membranes

We then wash the DNA repeatedly to get rid of excess protein and cellular debris. The enzyme Proteinase K is often used

An RNase enzyme is used to degrade RNA so that we only extract one type of nucleic acid (DNA)

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 9
slides.text:
2. DNA EXTRACTION
Caught in a net
You will extract DNA using a specialised silica membrane. It is very important you keep track of where your DNA is throughout the process!
The lysis buffer contains the detergent

The binding buffer has a high salt concentration, causing the DNA to stick to the silica membrane

The elution buffer lowers the salt concentration, releasing the DNA from the membrane

DNA in supernatant

DNA in pellet

DNA trapped in silica membrane

DNA in solution

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 10
slides.text:
2. DNA EXTRACTION
A quick check-up
After DNA extraction, it is important to check the purity of the yield and quantify the amount obtained

Together, these checks are usually referred to as DNA quantification, and can be performed by machines like the Biodrop

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 11
slides.text:
2. DNA AMPLIFICATION
Ready to multiply
As the last step of Practical 1, you will use some of your extracted DNA to set up a polymerase chain reaction

A left and right primer are needed to amplify the target region
The polymerase used comes from the heat-resistant bacterium Thermus aquaticus

You will also setup a no-template control (NTC) which contains all the PCR components but no template DNA (water instead)

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 12
Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 13
slides.text:
2. DNA AMPLIFICATION
Running up that gel
In practical 2, you will check whether your PCR reaction worked, and if you managed to keep your NTC free of contamination

You will receive an agarose gel that has solidified and is ready for use (part C in the diagram)

After loading your sample and your NTC, you’ll leave the gel to run for ~50 mins before returning to check.

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 14
slides.text:
2. DNA AMPLIFICATION
Snapping a pic
Once the gel has run for long enough, you will view the gel using a gel documentation system (gel doc)

The gel doc uses UV radiation to excite the dyes in the PCR reaction mixtures, allowing you to see how far the amplicons have moved. A molecular weight marker (ladder) is used to determine the size of the amplicons

The fully-labelled image of your gel must be included in your practical report

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 15
slides.text:
3. DNA SEQUENCING
Alphabet time
At the end of practical 2, you will set up a reaction to sequence your PCR amplicons

The set up is similar to PCR, but instead of setting up a template and no-template control, you’ll prepare forward and reverse reactions

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 16
slides.text:
4. DATA COMPARISON
Compare and despair
For practical 3, you will receive the sequence read from your amplified DNA fragment

The results will be in FASTA format (FAST Alignment) – a simple text file with one continuous sequence ‘wrapped’ into rows.

Your job will be to use bioinformatic tools to find where this sequence aligns against the human reference sequence, and what differences exist

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 17
slides.text:
4. DATA COMPARISON
Cause and effect
Once you have figured out the location of your PCR amplicon, and any differences to the reference genome, you will need to annotate these differences using standard mutation nomenclature

slides.topic: Medical Genetics Practical — From Sample to Sequence — source 18
slides.text:
5. TEST RESULTS/CONCLUSION
Reporting back
Once the consequences of any identified variants are known, it’s time to report back to the patient

In clear language suitable for both the GP and the patient, you need to explain how the test was conducted (methods), what the results were (results), what the results mean (interpretation), and what the patient/GP should do moving forward (recommendation)
